name: Edicts of Ashoka
info: A collection of more than thirty inscriptions on pillars, boulders and cave walls, attributed to the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent in the 3rd century BCE; they are the earliest written and datable texts from India.

facts.made: Attributed to Emperor Ashoka of the Mauryan Empire, who ruled from 268 to 232 BCE; engraved on his order, mostly in Prakrit, with some Greek and Aramaic versions in the northwest
facts.form: More than thirty inscriptions in four groups: Minor Rock Edicts, Minor Pillar Edicts, 14 Major Rock Edicts (with 2 separate ones in Odisha) and 7 Major Pillar Edicts; written in Ashokan Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic, in the Brahmi and Kharoshthi scripts and the Greek and Aramaic scripts
facts.where: On rocks, cave walls and pillars across modern India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Afghanistan and Pakistan; the Kandahar inscriptions stand in the city of Old Kandahar in Afghanistan
facts.known: the earliest written and datable texts from India; the policy of dhamma; the remorse after the Kalinga conquest; the Greek kings named in Major Rock Edict No. 13; the Rummindei Edict naming Lumbini as the Buddha's birthplace; early Brahmi numerals; their decipherment by James Prinsep in 1838

t: The edicts are the earliest written and datable texts from India, and because they were cut in stone they survive as they were first inscribed, unlike the Vedic texts, which were composed and handed down orally.

They set out a policy of dhamma, an ethic of non-violence, tolerance of all sects, obedience to parents and humane treatment of servants, which Romila Thapar describes as one to which no religious or social group could object.
The Brahmi and Kharoshthi scripts of the edicts had become extinct by about the 5th century CE, and were deciphered in the 1830s by Christian Lassen and James Prinsep.
dyk: In Minor Rock Edict No. 1 Ashoka says he had been on tour for 256 days, and the numeral 6 in that number is counted among the earliest ancestors of the digit used today.
ev: The Kandahar Bilingual Rock Inscription, in Greek and Aramaic, is written in the 10th year of Ashoka's reign at the border of his empire with the Hellenistic world
The Minor Pillar Edicts begin, from the 12th year of Ashoka's reign
Major Rock Edict No. 13, which names Hellenistic kings, is dated to about the 14th year of the reign
The Major Pillar Edicts are inscribed from the 26th and 27th years of the reign, the most technically elegant of the inscriptions
The Chinese traveller Fa Hian refers to one of Ashoka's pillar edicts at Ni-li, an edict that has not been found
Christian Lassen makes the first successful attempt to decipher Brahmi, using the bilingual Greek-Brahmi coins of Agathocles
James Prinsep publishes translations of a large number of rock edicts, after identifying the rest of the Brahmi characters
An inscription found at Maski confirms that the title Devanampiya belongs to Ashoka

sections.origins:
The edicts are attributed to Ashoka of the Mauryan Empire, who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from 268 BCE to 232 BCE. Another reckoning places his reign at 269 to 233 BCE. By the edicts' own account, the Kalinga conquest of the eighth year of his reign was the starting point for his remorse over the horrors of war and for his gradual conversion to Buddhism. The edicts name the Hellenistic kings who were his neighbours, and the Greek communities of the northwest, left after the conquests of Alexander the Great around 323 BCE, were still significant in his time.

Earlier Indian texts, such as the Vedic texts, were composed and handed down orally. Ashoka was probably the first Indian ruler to create stone inscriptions. Some scholars see Achaemenid influence on the edicts: the word lipi, which Ashoka used for his inscriptions, is thought to come from the Old Persian dipî, used by Darius I in the Behistun inscription, and the act of engraving edicts on rock may follow Achaemenid practice. It has also been suggested that the Delphic maxims inscribed at Ai-Khanoum around 300 BCE, which resemble the edicts in wording and content, may have influenced them.
sections.content:
The edicts fall into four categories by size and medium: Minor Rock Edicts, Minor Pillar Edicts, 14 Major Rock Edicts with 2 separate ones in Odisha, and 7 Major Pillar Edicts. Ashoka called them Dhaṃma Lipi, the inscriptions of the Dharma. The Minor Rock Edicts and Minor Pillar Edicts are very religious: they mention the Buddha, the Sangha and Buddhist scriptures, and Minor Rock Edict No. 3, found beside the Bairat Temple, lists sermons that monks, nuns and laypeople were to hear and meditate on. The Major Rock Edicts and Major Pillar Edicts never mention the Buddha. They are moral and political, concerned with order, proper behaviour, non-violence, the administration of the state and relations with foreign countries.

The dhamma they promote is described as largely ecumenical and non-sectarian. Romila Thapar lists its principles as non-violence, tolerance of all sects, obedience to parents, respect to brahmins and other religious teachers, liberality toward friends, humane treatment of servants and generosity towards all. Major Rock Edict No. 1 says that animals killed daily in the royal kitchen had fallen from many hundred thousands to three. Major Rock Edict No. 2 records medical treatment for men and cattle, and Major Rock Edict No. 12 says that those who praise their own sect and blame others injure their own sect severely. Major Rock Edict No. 13 names Antiochos, Ptolemy, Antigonos, Magas and Alexander as kings reached by the Dharma.
sections.making:
Three languages were used: Ashokan Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic, the last an official language of the former Achaemenid Empire. The Prakrit varied from early Gandhari in the northwest to Old Ardhamagadhi in the east, where it served as the chancery language of the court, and its register tends to be informal or colloquial. Prakrit was written in Brahmi and, in the area of modern Pakistan, Kharoshthi. The Greek of the Kandahar Greek Edict is of a very high level and shows philosophical refinement. In the south, in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, Ashoka used the Prakrit of the north and not the local Dravidian language, which has been interpreted as a kind of authoritarianism towards the newly conquered territories.

The inscriptions were located in public places and were meant for people to read. The Major Rock Edicts stand not in the Mauryan heartland, traditionally centred on Bihar, but on the frontiers. The earliest edicts are the Minor Rock Edicts, whose engraving is generally very poor; the Major Pillar Edicts of the 26th and 27th years are the most technically elegant. According to Irwin, the Sarnath and Sanchi pillar inscriptions were cut by inexperienced Indian engravers when stone engraving was still new in India, while the Sarnath capital was made under craftsmen from the former Achaemenid Empire.
sections.reception:
The Brahmi script and the Prakrit of the edicts remained in popular use through the Kushan period and could be read down to the 4th century CE, under the Gupta rulers. The edicts were thus there for everyone to see and understand for nearly 700 years, which suggests they remained influential for a long time. Their Prakrit is thought to have given Prakrit great prestige, so that it remained the main inscriptional language for centuries, until inscriptional Sanskrit rose from the 1st century CE. Around 400, the Chinese traveller Fa Hian wrote of an edict of Ashoka at Ni-li, which has not yet been found.

The edicts also state that Ashoka sent emissaries and medicinal plants to the Hellenistic kings. It is not clear from Hellenic records whether these emissaries were received or had any influence. Colonial-era scholars such as Rhys Davids attributed Ashoka's claims of conquest by the Dharma to vanity and doubted that Greeks could have been influenced by Indian thought. Other authors have noted parallels between Buddhism, Cyrenaicism and Epicureanism, and some suggest that Hegesias of Cyrene may have been influenced by Ashoka's missionaries. Louis Robert suggests that the emissaries to the western courts were Greek citizens of Kandahar. André Dupont-Sommer proposed that Ashoka's missions influenced the Essenes and Therapeutae. The evidence for Buddhists in the west at that time is very meagre.
sections.survival:
The Brahmi and Kharoshthi scripts both became extinct around the 5th century CE and were undeciphered when the edicts were discovered and investigated in the 19th century. Christian Lassen made the first successful attempts at Brahmi in 1836, using the bilingual Greek-Brahmi coins of the Indo-Greek king Agathocles. James Prinsep, an official of the East India Company, identified the rest of the characters with the help of Major Cunningham and published his results in March 1838. Richard Salomon calls his rendering of the Brahmi alphabet virtually perfect. Prinsep deciphered Kharoshthi in parallel with Lassen, using bilingual Greek-Kharoshthi coinage. The Greek and Aramaic inscriptions were discovered only in the 20th century.

Prinsep first assumed that the King Devanampriya Piyadasi of the edicts was a Sri Lankan king, and then linked the title to Ashoka through Pali material from Sri Lanka communicated by George Turnour. An inscription found in 1915 by C. Beadon at Maski confirmed the identification, and another at Gujarra gives Devanampiya Piyadasi Asokaraja. Christopher I. Beckwith proposed that Piyadasi, author of the major edicts, and Ashoka, named in the minor ones, were different rulers; his theories are not accepted by mainstream scholarship. Patrick Olivelle calls the theory an outlier that no mainstream Ashokan scholar would subscribe to.
sections.legacy:
The edicts provide the first tangible evidence of Buddhism. The Rummindei Edict records Ashoka's visit to Lumbini and names it as the birthplace of the Buddha, and uses for the first time in historical records the epithet Sakyamuni. Ashoka was probably the first Indian ruler to create stone inscriptions, and in doing so began an important Indian tradition of royal epigraphical inscriptions. The earliest known stone inscriptions in Sanskrit date from the 1st century BCE.

The first examples of the Hindu–Arabic numeral system appear in the Brahmi numerals of the edicts. The system was not yet positional: the zero and a mature positional system came around the 6th century CE. The modern glyph for 6 evolved in a rather straightforward way from the numeral in Minor Rock Edict No. 1. Scholars also note that the edicts reflect the desire of rulers more than actual events: a fine of 100 panas for poaching deer in imperial hunting preserves shows that rule-breakers existed. The wildlife provisions have led some to call Ashoka perhaps the first ruler in history to advocate conservation measures. Thapar suggests that the dhamma could also act as a focus of loyalty to weld together the diverse strands of the empire.

summary: The Edicts of Ashoka are more than thirty inscriptions on pillars, boulders and cave walls, attributed to the Mauryan emperor Ashoka. They set out his policy of dhamma and are the earliest written and datable texts from India. James Prinsep deciphered their Brahmi script in 1838.
references: Eugen Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka. New Edition by E. Hultzsch (Clarendon Press, 1925)
Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy: A Guide to the Study of Inscriptions in Sanskrit, Prakrit, and the other Indo-Aryan Languages (Oxford University Press, 1998)
notes: The article gives Ashoka's reign as 268-232 BCE in most places and 269-233 BCE once (Minor Rock Edicts); I used 268-232 and mentioned the other once in origins. start -260 is the Kandahar bilingual inscription, the first known edict (year 10).
The article contradicts itself on the date of the Rummindei and Nigali Sagar pillars (19th and 20th year in one place, Rummindei visit in the 21st year elsewhere): left out of the text and events.

The article gives the Major Pillar Edicts as 237-236 BCE (years 26 and 27) and says the Minor Pillar Edicts began 256 BCE (year 12) while Major Rock Edict 13 is c. 256-255 BCE; ordering of events follows those.

Left out: the Gandhari and Greek-king equivalence list in detail, quoted translations beyond short paraphrases, the claim that the Dharma 'reached as far as' the Mediterranean as plain fact, the Mahavamsa missionary account, the Fa Hian quotation text (only the reference to an edict is used). 'About 400' for Fa Hian follows the article's '400 A.D.'. The ev label 'c. 400' has no era marker by design (CE).
The article's remark that the Kandahar Greek is of very high level and philosophical refinement is kept as the article's; the 'authoritarianism' reading is hedged as an interpretation.
